q1: SELECT ITM.ITEMN, ITPV.VENDN FROM ITM ITM, (SELECT DISTINCT ITP.ITEMN, PUR.VENDN FROM ITP ITP, PUR PUR WHERE ITP.PONUM = PUR.PONUM AND PUR.ODATE > 85) ITPV WHERE ITM.ITEMN = ITPV.ITEMN AND ITM.ITEMN > 1 AND ITM.ITEMN < 20
q2: SELECT DISTINCT ITM.ITEMN, PUR.VENDN FROM ITM ITM, ITP ITP, PUR PUR WHERE ITP.PONUM = PUR.PONUM AND ITM.ITEMN = ITP.ITEMN AND PUR.ODATE > 85 AND ITM.ITEMN > 1 AND ITM.ITEMN < 20
explanation: Both queries aim to select unique combinations of ITEMN and VENDN from the ITM, ITP, and PUR tables with similar join conditions and filters. Q1 involves a subquery with distinct selection before joining with ITM. Q2 directly joins all three tables with a distinct selection. Both result in the same final unique pairs with the given conditions.

q1: SELECT Z.A, Z.B FROM R1 X, R2 Y, R2 Z WHERE X.A = Y.A AND Y.A = Z.A AND X.A = Z.A AND Y.B = Z.B
q2: SELECT Z.A, Z.B FROM R1 X, R2 Y, R2 Z WHERE X.A = Y.A AND Y.A = Z.A AND X.A = Z.A
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are not equivalent because Q1 has an additional condition (Y.B = Z.B) that is not present in Q2. This condition affects the result by further restricting the matching rows from tables R2 (Y and Z). If there is a mismatch in the B field between Y and Z for the same A, Q1 will not return those rows, whereas Q2 will.
counterexample_dsp: Use a test database where R1 and R2 tables have common values in the A column but different values in the B column for R2 rows with the same A.

q1: SELECT ITEMPRICE.NP, ITM.TYPE, ITM.ITEMNO FROM (SELECT DISTINCT ITP.ITEMNO AS ITN, ITP.NP AS NP FROM ITP ITP WHERE ITP.NP > 1000) ITEMPRICE, ITM ITM WHERE ITEMPRICE.ITN = ITM.ITEMNO
q2: SELECT DISTINCT ITP.NP, ITM.TYPE, ITM.ITEMNO FROM ITP ITP, ITM ITM WHERE ITP.NP > 1000 AND ITP.ITEMNO = ITM.ITEMNO
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are not equivalent because Q1 selects distinct ITEMNO from ITP first, then joins with ITM, while Q2 does the join first and then selects distinct rows. This results in different row eliminations when there are multiple entries in ITP with the same ITEMNO but different NP values.
counterexample_dsp: A counterexample occurs when there are multiple rows in ITP with the same ITEMNO where at least one of them meets the NP > 1000 condition and they have different NP values.

q1: SELECT ITM.ITEMNO, ITEMPRICE.NP FROM (SELECT DISTINCT ITP.ITEMNO AS ITN, ITP.NP AS NP FROM ITP ITP) ITEMPRICE, ITM ITM WHERE ITEMPRICE.ITN = ITM.ITEMNO
q2: SELECT DISTINCT ITM.ITEMNO, ITP.NP FROM ITP ITP, ITM ITM WHERE ITP.ITEMNO = ITM.ITEMNO
explanation: Q1 and Q2 achieve the same objective: obtaining a list of ITEMNO and NP pairs where ITEMNO exists in both the ITP and ITM tables. Q1 uses a subquery with DISTINCT which does not change the result because it already aligns with the DISTINCT in the main query, making both queries effectively equivalent in output.

q1: SELECT * FROM ITP ITP WHERE ITP.ITEMN IN (SELECT ITL.ITEMN FROM ITL ITL WHERE ITL.WKCEN = 468 AND ITL.LOCAN = 0)
q2: SELECT DISTINCT ITP.* FROM ITP ITP, ITL ITL WHERE ITP.ITEMN = ITL.ITEMN AND ITL.WKCEN = 468 AND ITL.LOCAN = 0
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are semantically equivalent. Both queries aim to select all columns from the ITP table where the ITEMN exists in the set of ITEMNs that satisfy ITL.WKCEN = 468 and ITL.LOCAN = 0. Although Q2 uses a JOIN and DISTINCT to prevent duplicates, Q1 inherently prevents duplicates as ITEMN is a primary key. Hence, they effectively produce the same results.

q1: SELECT T.TMEMBER FROM DEPTS D, TEAMS T WHERE D.DPROJ = T.TPROJ AND D.DNAME = 'SECURITY'
q2: SELECT V1.E FROM (SELECT D.DNAME AS D, D.DPROJ AS P, P.EMPL AS E FROM DEPTS D, PAYROLL P WHERE D.DNAME = P.PDEPT) V1, (SELECT T.TMEMBER AS E, P.PDEPT AS D, T.TPROJ AS P FROM TEAMS T, PAYROLL P WHERE T.TMEMBER = P.EMPL) V2 WHERE V1.D = 'SECURITY' AND V1.P = V2.P AND V1.E = V2.E AND V1.D = V2.D

q2: SELECT X.B AS XB FROM R X WHERE X.A < 10

q1:
SELECT 
    P.UID,
    P.UNAME,
    COALESCE(Q.CNT, 0) AS CNT
FROM (
    SELECT X.UID, X.UNAME
    FROM USER X
    WHERE X.CITY = 3
) AS P
LEFT JOIN (
    SELECT Y.UID, COUNT(*) AS CNT
    FROM PICTURE Y
    WHERE Y.SIZE > 1000000
    GROUP BY Y.UID
) AS Q
USING (UID);
q2: SELECT X.UID AS UID, X.UNAME AS UNAME, COUNT(*) AS CNT FROM USER X, PICTURE Y WHERE X.UID = Y.UID AND Y.SIZE > 1000000 AND X.CITY = 3 GROUP BY X.UID, X.UNAME
schema:
CREATE TABLE USER (UID INT, UNAME INT, CITY INT);
CREATE TABLE PICTURE (UID INT, SIZE INT);
explanation: Q1 includes all users from city 3, even those who have no pictures larger than 1000000 in size, due to the LEFT JOIN with a COALESCE function setting missing counts to 0. In contrast, Q2 only considers users with at least one picture larger than 1000000, as it uses an INNER JOIN logic by implicitly joining with the WHERE clause. Therefore, Q1 can return more rows with zero counts for certain users.
counterexample: INSERT INTO USER (UID, UNAME, CITY) VALUES (1, 'Alice', 3); INSERT INTO USER (UID, UNAME, CITY) VALUES (2, 'Bob', 3); INSERT INTO PICTURE (UID, SIZE) VALUES (1, 900000); INSERT INTO PICTURE (UID, SIZE) VALUES (2, 1500000);
counterexample_dsp: Database where a user from city 3 has no pictures over 1000000 in size; Q1 returns this user with count 0, while Q2 does not list this user at all.

q2: SELECT X.PNUM AS XP FROM PARTS X, (SELECT Y.PNUM AS SUPPNUM, COUNT(Y.SHIPDATE) AS CT FROM SUPPLY Y WHERE Y.SHIPDATE < 10 GROUP BY Y.PNUM) TEMP WHERE X.QOH = TEMP.CT AND X.PNUM = TEMP.SUPPNUM

q1: SELECT X.NAME AS XN FROM EMP X WHERE (X.EMP, X.DEPT) IN (SELECT Y.MGR, Y.DEPT FROM DEPT Y WHERE Y.LOC = 3)

q1: SELECT DISTINCT X.X AS AX FROM A X, B Y WHERE X.YA = Y.YB
q2:
SELECT X.X AS AX
FROM A X, A Y, B Z
WHERE X.X = Y.X
  AND X.YA = Z.YB

UNION ALL

SELECT 1 AS AX
FROM A X
WHERE 1 = 0;
schema:
CREATE TABLE A (X INT, YA INT);
CREATE TABLE B (YB INT);
explanation: Q1 retrieves distinct values of X.X from table A that have matching YB values in table B, while Q2 performs a similar join and adds an unnecessary self-join on A to ensure rows are unique, then unions with an always-empty result set. These differences in operations can lead Q1 and Q2 to return differing result sets under specific data configurations.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO A (X, YA) VALUES (1, 10);
INSERT INTO B (YB) VALUES (10);
counterexample_dsp: For Q1 to return a non-empty result while Q2 returns an empty result, A must have a row where X.X matches a row in B based on X.YA = B.YB, but there's no pair in A where X.X appear multiple times (additional row in Q2 sel join condition).

q1: SELECT X.X AS AX FROM A X WHERE X.YX = 'HELLO'
q2: SELECT X.X AS AX FROM A X WHERE X.YX = 'HELLO HI'

explanation: Q1 and Q2 are not equivalent because they filter rows based on different string values in the YX column. Q1 looks for rows where YX equals 'HELLO', while Q2 looks for rows where YX equals 'HELLO HI'. These conditions will result in different outputs unless the YX column contains both strings, and no other values.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO A (X, YA, YX) VALUES (1, 10, 'HELLO');
INSERT INTO A (X, YA, YX) VALUES (2, 20, 'HELLO HI');
counterexample_dsp: A test database where the table A contains rows that have the YX column value that matches one query's condition but not the other's.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT X.X AS X FROM R1 X, R2 Y WHERE X.Y = Y.Y AND X.X = 1
q2: SELECT DISTINCT X.X AS X FROM R1 X, R1 Y, R2 Z WHERE X.X = Y.X AND X.Y = Z.Y AND X.X = 1
schema:
CREATE TABLE R1 (X INT, Y INT);
CREATE TABLE R2 (Y INT);
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are not equivalent because Q2 imposes an additional self-join on table R1 requiring X.X to match Y.X, which is not a requirement in Q1.
counterexample_dsp: The difference is triggered when there are multiple rows in R1 with the same X value but different Y values, where one matches a row in R2.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT * FROM R X WHERE X.A1 = X.A2 AND X.A2 = X.A3
q2: SELECT DISTINCT * FROM R X WHERE X.A1 = X.A2 AND X.A1 = X.A3
schema: CREATE TABLE R (A1 INT, A2 INT, A3 INT);
explanation: Both Q1 and Q2 select rows from table R where the three columns A1, A2, and A3 have the same values. Thus, they are equivalent.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT X.* FROM R X, R Y
q2: SELECT DISTINCT X.* FROM R X
schema: CREATE TABLE R (X INT);
explanation: Q1 performs a cross join of table R with itself, while Q2 simply selects distinct rows from R. If R has more than one row, Q1 can produce multiple identical rows before the DISTINCT clause is applied, potentially leading to different results compared to Q2 which directly applies DISTINCT on the rows of R.
counterexample: INSERT INTO R (X) VALUES (1); INSERT INTO R (X) VALUES (1);
counterexample_dsp: If table R contains more than one row with the same value, Q1 will generate more combinations due to the self-join, but Q2 will simply return the distinct rows. For instance, if R has multiple rows with value 1, Q1 can produce several redundant results before DISTINCT applies, while Q2 uniformly applies DISTINCT at the outset.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT Y.A AS A FROM R X, R Y WHERE X.A = Y.A
q2: SELECT DISTINCT X.A AS A FROM R X
schema: CREATE TABLE R (A INT);
explanation: Q1 returns the distinct values of A from R where there is at least one other row having the same value of A, while Q2 returns all distinct values of A from R regardless of duplicates.
counterexample: INSERT INTO R VALUES (1);
counterexample_dsp: If the table R contains a single row, Q1 will return an empty result since there is no other row with the same A value, but Q2 will return the distinct A value from that single row.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT Y.A1 AS A1, Y.A2 AS A2 FROM R X, R Y WHERE X.A1 = Y.A1 AND X.A2 = Y.A2
q2: SELECT DISTINCT X.A1 AS A1, X.A2 AS A2 FROM R X
schema: CREATE TABLE R (A1 INT, A2 INT);
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are not equivalent because Q1 filters results based on pairs existing in a self-join of the table, while Q2 returns all unique pairs in the table.
counterexample: INSERT INTO R (A1, A2) VALUES (1, 2); INSERT INTO R (A1, A2) VALUES (1, 2);
counterexample_dsp: If table R has duplicate rows, Q1 will not include a row that is a duplicate whereas Q2 will include distinct rows.

q1: SELECT X.A, SUM(X.A + X.B) FROM R X GROUP BY X.A
q2: SELECT Y.A, SUM(Y.A + Y.B) FROM R Y GROUP BY Y.A
schema: CREATE TABLE R (A INT, B INT);
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are semantically equivalent. Both queries calculate the sum of the expression (A + B) for each group of rows in table R aggregated by the same column A. The naming of the table aliases X and Y does not impact the underlying logic or output of the queries. Therefore, they produce identical results.

q1: SELECT * FROM (SELECT * FROM R X WHERE X.X > 50) Y WHERE Y.X < 200
q2: SELECT * FROM (SELECT * FROM R X WHERE X.X < 200) Y WHERE Y.X > 50
schema: CREATE TABLE R (X INT);
explanation: Both Q1 and Q2 filter the rows from table R, retaining only those where X is greater than 50 and less than 200. The order of applying these filters does not affect the final result, resulting in equivalent queries.

q1: SELECT * FROM R X WHERE X.X > 50 AND X.X < 200
q2: SELECT * FROM (SELECT * FROM R X WHERE X.X > 50) Y WHERE Y.X < 200
schema: CREATE TABLE R (X INT);
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are semantically equivalent as both apply the same filter conditions on the table R. The subquery in Q2 does not change the logic of the filtering applied by the WHERE clause.

q1: SELECT COUNT(*) AS A FROM R X
q2: SELECT COUNT(Y.B) FROM R Y
schema: CREATE TABLE R (A INT, B INT);
explanation: Q1 counts all rows in table R, while Q2 counts only the rows where the column B is not NULL.
counterexample: INSERT INTO R (A, B) VALUES (1, NULL); INSERT INTO R (A, B) VALUES (2, 3);
counterexample_dsp: A difference arises when there are NULL values in column B. For Q1, all rows are counted, regardless of NULLs. Q2 doesn't count rows where B is NULL.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT * FROM R X WHERE X.X > 50 OR X.X < 200
schema: CREATE TABLE R (X INT);
explanation: Q1 applies DISTINCT after applying a single WHERE condition, whereas Q2 takes values from two WHERE conditions and applies DISTINCT after a UNION ALL. This can result in duplicate values being retained in Q2, potentially leading to different results.
counterexample: INSERT INTO R (X) VALUES (100), (200);
counterexample_dsp: If the value of 'X' is between 50 and 200, then in Q2, that value would be selected twice from two sub-queries in the UNION ALL operation, but only one copy will be in the final result due to DISTINCT. If equal to 50 or 200, it only satisfies one sub-query, that value will appear only once in Q2. Q1 considers such values once. This duplication difference will lead to different results in Q1 and Q2.

q1: SELECT DEPT.NAME AS DNAME, COUNT(*) AS C FROM DEPT AS DEPT GROUP BY DEPT.NAME HAVING DEPT.NAME = 10
q2: SELECT T2.DNAME, T2.CNT AS C FROM (SELECT DEPT0.NAME AS DNAME, COUNT(*) AS CNT FROM DEPT AS DEPT0 GROUP BY DEPT0.NAME) AS T2 WHERE T2.DNAME = 10
schema: CREATE TABLE DEPT (DEPTNO INT, NAME INT);
explanation: Both queries Q1 and Q2 are semantically equivalent as they are effectively performing the same operation: counting the entries in the DEPT table where the NAME equals 10, and returning the count grouped by NAME. The 'HAVING' clause in Q1 and the 'WHERE' clause in Q2 filter results in the same way, ensuring only those groups where NAME equals 10 are included in the result. The aliases and subquery structure in Q2 do not alter the logic.

q1: SELECT * FROM (SELECT * FROM R X WHERE X.X > 0) Y WHERE Y.X > 0
q2: SELECT * FROM R X WHERE X.X > 0
schema: CREATE TABLE R (X INT);
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are equivalent. Both queries retrieve all rows from the table R where the value of X is greater than 0. The subquery in Q1 does not alter the result, as it applies the same condition (X > 0) as the outer query.

q1: SELECT * FROM A X WHERE X.C IN (SELECT Y.C FROM A Y)
q2: SELECT * FROM A X
schema: CREATE TABLE A (C INT);
explanation: Both Q1 and Q2 are equivalent because Q1 selects rows from table A where the value of column C is in the set of values from column C of table A, which is always true if there are no NULL values or other constraints affecting visibility. Thus, Q1 and Q2 will return the same set of rows from A.

q1: SELECT X.A1 AS A1, X.A2 AS A2, Y.B1 AS B1, Y.B2 AS B2 FROM A X, B Y WHERE X.A1 = Y.B1
q2: SELECT Y.A1 AS A1, Y.A2 AS A2, X.B1 AS B1, X.B2 AS B2 FROM B X, A Y WHERE Y.A1 = X.B1
schema:

explanation: Q1 and Q2 are equivalent because they perform the same join operation between tables A and B on the same condition X.A1 = Y.B1 or Y.A1 = X.B1 and select corresponding columns. The renaming of variables X and Y, as well as their use across both queries, maintains the logical consistency. Hence, they yield the same result sets.

q1: SELECT * FROM R1 X, (SELECT * FROM R2 UNION ALL SELECT * FROM R3) Y
explanation: The queries Q1 and Q2 are not equivalent because Q1 performs a cross join between R1 and the union of R2 and R3, while Q2 performs two separate cross joins with R2 and R3 and then unions their results.
counterexample_dsp: Q1 will return more rows because it allows for combinations between all elements of R1 and the combined set of R2 and R3. On the other hand, Q2 generates combinations separately for R1 with R2 and R1 with R3.

q1: SELECT X.B AS XB, Y.B AS YB FROM R1 X, R2 Y
q2: SELECT X1.XB AS XB, Y1.YB AS YB FROM (SELECT X.B AS XB FROM R1 X) X1, (SELECT Y.B AS YB FROM R2 Y) Y1
schema:
CREATE TABLE R1 (A INT, B INT);
CREATE TABLE R2 (A INT, B INT);
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are equivalent because both queries perform a Cartesian product between tables R1 and R2, and then select the B column from each table. Q2 uses subqueries to rename the columns, but the output remains the same as Q1, which directly specifies the column aliases.

q1: SELECT * FROM (SELECT * FROM R UNION ALL SELECT * FROM S) X
schema:
CREATE TABLE R (X INT);
CREATE TABLE S (X INT);
explanation: Both Q1 and Q2 output all rows from the union of tables R and S without eliminating duplicates, hence they are semantically equivalent.

q1: SELECT * FROM A X, (SELECT * FROM B Y WHERE Y.X < 100) Z WHERE X.X = Z.X
q2: SELECT * FROM A X, B Y WHERE X.X = Y.X AND Y.X < 100

CREATE TABLE B (X INT);
explanation: Both Q1 and Q2 perform a join between tables A and B on the condition that the 'X' value from both tables are equal and also apply the condition that the 'X' value in table B is less than 100. Q1 uses a subquery to filter table B before the join, while Q2 applies the filter directly during the join. Despite the different approaches, they achieve the same result.

q1: SELECT X.A AS A FROM X X, Y Y WHERE X.K = Y.K
q2: SELECT X1.A AS X1A FROM (SELECT X.A AS A, X.K AS K FROM X X) X1, Y Y WHERE X1.K = Y.K
schema:
CREATE TABLE X (A INT, K INT);
CREATE TABLE Y (A INT, K INT);
explanation: Both Q1 and Q2 perform an inner join between tables X and Y based on the column K and select the column A from table X. Q2 demonstrates this by using a subquery that effectively does nothing to alter the outcome, as it selects the same columns used in Q1. Hence, both queries are equivalent.

q1: SELECT * FROM R1 X, (SELECT * FROM R2 Y WHERE Y.X > 0) Z
q2: SELECT * FROM R1 X, R2 Y WHERE Y.X > 0
schema:
CREATE TABLE R1 (X INT);
CREATE TABLE R2 (X INT);
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are equivalent because both queries join all rows from R1 with rows from R2 that satisfy the condition Y.X > 0. The subquery in Q1 is an inline view that filters R2 rows with the same condition as the WHERE clause in Q2. This results in the same outcome, as the condition applied and the join structure are effectively identical in both queries.

q1: SELECT X.A + X.B, X.A/X.B AS A FROM R X
q2: SELECT Y.A + Y.B, Y.A/Y.B AS A FROM R Y
schema: CREATE TABLE R (A INT, B INT);
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are semantically equivalent because they perform the same operations under the same conditions; the only difference lies in the alias used for the table, which does not affect the logic or result of the queries.

q1: SELECT * FROM A X UNION ALL SELECT * FROM A X WHERE FALSE
q2: SELECT * FROM A X
schema: CREATE TABLE A (X INT);
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are semantically equivalent. Q1 selects all records from table A using UNION ALL with another selection from table A that yields no results due to the WHERE FALSE condition, effectively returning the same result as Q2, which selects all records from table A.

q1: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, SUM(C.CREDITS) FROM COURSE C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING SUM(C.CREDITS) > 10 AND COUNT(DISTINCT C.CREDITS) > 5
q2: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, SUM(C.CREDITS) FROM COURSE C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING SUM(C.CREDITS) > 10 AND COUNT(DISTINCT C.CREDITS) > 8
explanation: The two queries differ in the threshold for COUNT(DISTINCT C.CREDITS) in the HAVING clause. Q1 requires more than 5 distinct CREDITS values, while Q2 requires more than 8 distinct CREDITS values. This means Q2 is more restrictive, and as such, it will produce fewer or equal results compared to Q1 when the other condition SUM(C.CREDITS) > 10 is met.
counterexample_dsp: Consider a scenario where a department has courses accumulating a total of 15 credits with exactly 6 distinct credit values. q1: WITH S AS (SELECT ID, TIME_SLOT_ID, YEAR FROM TAKES NATURAL JOIN SECTION GROUP BY ID, TIME_SLOT_ID, YEAR HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT TIME_SLOT_ID)>4) SELECT DISTINCT ID,NAME FROM S NATURAL JOIN STUDENT
q2: WITH S AS (SELECT ID, TIME_SLOT_ID, YEAR FROM TAKES NATURAL JOIN SECTION GROUP BY ID, TIME_SLOT_ID, YEAR HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT TIME_SLOT_ID)>5) SELECT DISTINCT ID,NAME FROM S NATURAL JOIN STUDENT
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are not equivalent because they have different conditions for filtering the students. Q1 selects students who have taken classes in more than 4 distinct time slots, whereas Q2 selects students who have taken classes in more than 5 distinct time slots.
counterexample_dsp: In a small test database, if a student has taken classes in exactly 5 distinct time slots, they will appear in the results of Q1 but not in Q2.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT DEPT_NAME FROM COURSE WHERE CREDITS=(SELECT MAX(CREDITS) FROM COURSE)
q2: SELECT DISTINCT DEPT_NAME FROM COURSE AS C JOIN (SELECT MAX(CREDITS) AS MAX_CREDITS FROM COURSE GROUP BY DEPT_NAME) AS A WHERE C.CREDITS = A.MAX_CREDITS
explanation: Q1 retrieves the department names for courses with the maximum credits across the entire COURSE table, while Q2 retrieves department names for courses with the maximum credits within each department. This difference in the scope of maximum credits calculation results in Q1 and Q2 not being equivalent.
counterexample: INSERT INTO COURSE (COURSE_ID, TITLE, DEPT_NAME, CREDITS) VALUES (1, 101, 1, 5); INSERT INTO COURSE (COURSE_ID, TITLE, DEPT_NAME, CREDITS) VALUES (2, 102, 1, 7); INSERT INTO COURSE (COURSE_ID, TITLE, DEPT_NAME, CREDITS) VALUES (3, 103, 2, 4); INSERT INTO COURSE (COURSE_ID, TITLE, DEPT_NAME, CREDITS) VALUES (4, 104, 2, 7);
counterexample_dsp: A COURSE table where two departments have courses, each with a different maximum credits. One maximum is the overall highest, and the other is the departmental highest only.
